vignette:
She is 68, an African woman who has been married for most of her adult life, and when she speaks about the worst years of that marriage, she does so in a voice that is steady at first, almost practical, as if she is telling someone how to prepare a meal. Only after a while does the strain show. She says there was never one single terrible night that stood apart from the others at the beginning. Instead, the violence entered her life gradually, after years of small humiliations, accusations, and controlling rules. Her husband decided who she could visit, what she could spend, when she was being "disrespectful." By the time he first hit her hard enough to leave bruises on her upper arms, she had already become used to watching his moods the way other people watch the weather.

She remembers one evening especially clearly. He had come home angry and suspicious, convinced she had shamed him by speaking too freely with neighbors. The argument moved quickly, as so many of them did, from words to force. He pushed her into a chair, slapped her across the face, then kicked her when she fell. She remembers the sound of something metal hitting the floor, her own breath catching, the heat in her chest, and the strange thought that she must not cry too loudly because the children might hear. In her memory, time narrows around details: the pattern in the curtain, the smell of sweat, the ache in her ribs when she tried to rise. Afterward, she sat very still, dizzy and ashamed, listening for his footsteps in the next room.

What follows is not one isolated attack but years of repeated beatings and threats. She learns to make herself smaller. She speaks softly, moves carefully, keeps rooms orderly because disorder can set him off. At night she lies awake listening for the turn of a key, trying to guess from the way he closes the door whether she will be safe until morning. During the day she functions as if nothing is wrong. She cooks, cleans, tends to the needs of the family, and tells herself that endurance is the same thing as strength. She is not employed outside the home, and over time her world becomes even smaller. Without her own income, leaving feels impossible. She depends on him materially while fearing him physically, and this dependence becomes its own kind of trap.

Even now, years later, she lives as though danger can erupt without warning. Loud male voices make her whole body tighten. If a door slams in the building, she startles so sharply that she has to hold onto furniture to steady herself. She says her heart begins racing before she has even had time to think. Sometimes, while washing dishes or folding clothes, she is seized by a vivid image of him standing over her, and for a moment she is no longer in the present kitchen but back in that older one, bracing for the next blow. She hates these moments because they arrive uninvited and leave her shaky and exhausted.

Sleep is poor. She dreads the night because that is when memories come closest. She wakes from dreams in which she is trying to scream and no sound comes out, or dreams in which she is trapped in a room with no door. Her husband may be in another part of the home, or even asleep beside her, but in those moments she feels as if the abuse is happening again. Sometimes she gets out of bed and sits fully dressed in a chair until dawn, unable to relax enough to lie down.

She avoids anything that might stir the past, though the effort takes much of her energy. She does not like speaking about her marriage with relatives or friends because she fears disbelief, pity, and gossip. She avoids television scenes of domestic conflict. She rarely attends social gatherings now, especially if men will be drinking. Her world has become organized around prevention: preventing anger, preventing attention, preventing memory. She knows this has made her isolated, but isolation feels safer than exposure.

There is also a grief she returns to often-the grief of the life she imagined she would have. She speaks about herself as if some essential part of her confidence was worn away over the years. She used to enjoy laughter, conversation, church events, and visits with neighbors. Now she finds herself mistrusting people's intentions and expecting criticism even in ordinary exchanges. When someone speaks sharply, she immediately assumes she has done something wrong. She is often on guard, scanning faces and tones of voice for signs of danger. By the end of the day she feels tired in a way that is more than physical.

In sessions, what stands out is how much of her present life is still organized around surviving what happened. She describes herself as "always prepared," but the preparation costs her peace. Even in quiet moments, she is rarely at ease. Part of her knows she is an older woman now, no longer living in those early years of marriage, yet her body does not seem to believe that the danger has passed. She lives with the past close to the surface, carried not as a story that is over, but as something her mind and body continue to expect.
